text: As the winter went on, society gradually accepted the strange arrangement, and Waythorn himself began to treat it as a matter of business rather than of feeling. <break time="0.8s" /> He came to see himself as one shareholder in a syndicate, with Haskett and Varick as his partners in the ownership of his wifes personality. <break time="0.8s" /> It was better, he decided with a wry smile, to own a third of a wife who knew how to make a man happy than a whole one who did not. <break time="0.8s" /> One afternoon Haskett was waiting in the library to speak with Alice about Lily when Varick arrived to see Waythorn on a matter of business and was shown into the same room. <break time="0.8s" /> When Waythorn joined them, the three men stood in an awkward silence, none of them knowing whether to sit down, to make conversation, or simply to leave. <break time="0.8s" /> Then the door opened, and Alice came in, greeting Varick with a note of pleasure and Haskett a shade less warmly, as though nothing could be more natural. <break time="0.8s" /> Shall we have tea in here, dear, she asked her husband, and with perfect composure she began to pour the tea while the three men watched in silence. <break time="0.8s" /> She handed a cup to each of her guests, and so smoothly did she manage the moment that the awkwardness in the room seemed to melt away. <break time="0.8s" /> Then she glanced about for her husband, and Waythorn, seeing at last the comedy of his own position, took the third cup with a laugh.
